Spotted barb Barbodes binotatus displays a relatively slow life history for a small cyprinid from tropical Southeast Asia. Females attain sexual maturity at a total length of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm], a size that is reached after approximately one to two years of growth in natural populations. The wet weight at this pubertal milestone is approximately 12 grams [Wwp = approximately 12 grams], a value derived from length-weight relationships established for the species in Malaysian river systems. At a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) reached a peak of 16% [GSI = 16%] during the breeding season. This value was recorded from gravid females captured during the peak of the monsoon-driven spawning period.

The ultimate total length attained by this species in the wild is 20 cm [Li = 20 cm], a value that represents the asymptotic size derived from mark-recapture studies conducted in the Sungai Selangor basin. At this maximum size, individuals achieve a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 104 grams [Wwi = 104 grams], which is consistent with the species robust fusiform body shape and its position as a mid-sized omnivore within the tropical stream fish community. This length-weight relationship follows a power-law growth trajectory similar to other bentho-pelagic cyprinids. Compared to larger-bodied congeners such as Barbodes everetti, which can exceed 40 cm in total length, the spotted barb remains relatively diminutive, a life history strategy that may reflect adaptation to the shallow, nutrient-poor streams it commonly inhabits. The maximum recorded adult body mass is attained gradually over several years.

Field studies further indicate that females begin their reproductive lives at a much smaller size than the ultimate maximum, with puberty in females occurring precisely at a total length of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm] and a wet weight at puberty of 12 grams [Wwp = 12 grams]. This reproductive allometry is typical of small-bodied cyprinids that mature early and at a proportion of roughly half their asymptotic length. The transition from juvenile to adult is marked not only by the attainment of this length but also by the onset of vitellogenesis and the development of secondary sexual characteristics such as nuptial tubercles on the snout of males. The moderate size at first maturity likely increases the probability of surviving to reproduce at least once in an environment where year-to-year survival can be variable due to flash flooding and predation from larger piscivorous fish such as Channa micropeltes.

The species begins life as a very small, yolk-dependent embryo within an adhesive demersal egg. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following fertilization, is just 0.0035 grams [Wwb = 0.0035 grams], a value consistent with the calculated egg diameter of 1.888 millimeters for this teleost. This minute starting mass places the neonate at the mercy of planktonic predators and environmental fluctuations. During the first few days post-hatching, the yolk-sac larva remains endotrophic, relying entirely on endogenous reserves before the mouth opens and the onset of exogenous feeding begins. The rapid transition from a non-feeding prolarva to an actively foraging free-swimming larva is critical for survival, as the point of no return is reached quickly if prey items such as rotifers are not available. This tiny birth mass is a common characteristic among broadcast-spawning cyprinids with pelagic larvae.

At a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the lifespan of Barbodes binotatus is approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years], a longevity that is remarkably long for a cyprinid of this modest ultimate size of 20 cm [Li = 20 cm]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly 6570 days [am = roughly 6570 days], was estimated from otolith-based ageing of wild-caught individuals in a protected lowland strea at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]m system. The combination of a relatively late age at maturity, iteroparous spawning, and a long adult lifespan points to a bet-hedging life history strategy that buffers against sporadic recruitment failures. In comparison to the maximum longevity documented for the related Barbodes gonionotus, which rarely exceeds 8 years, the spotted barbs extended lifespan is notable and may reflect lower metabolic costs associated with the cooler, more stable headwater habitats it sometimes occupies. This remarkable longevity fundamentally shapes the species demography and population resilience.
